813.title: Singing the verses
813.hook: these poems were memorized and chanted for centuries before being written down
813.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, texts are memorized in Pali and chanted in a steady intoned style, the kind of chant the Vinaya allows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the week closed with a crowd of voices, each kept in its own temper. Today, how those voices reached anyone at all.

Before dawn, in the Buddha's dwelling, a teacher turns to a visiting monk and says, let the teaching come to you to speak. And the monk begins to recite from memory, in a steady, intoned voice, a whole chapter of verses, start to finish, while the teacher listens. It's in the Udana, and in the Vinaya too. Nobody in the story opens a book. Today, the elders' songs as they first lived: in the mouth and the ear.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, A MONK RECITES.` → `NO BOOK TO OPEN.` → `IN THE MOUTH AND THE EAR.`

segments.voice: First, who's reciting. His name is Sona too, Sona Kutikanna, a different monk from the Sona with the bleeding feet. He has traveled a long way to see the Buddha, and they spend the night in the same dwelling. At dawn, invited, he intones a chapter of verses from the Sutta Nipata. When he finishes, the Buddha praises him: good, monk, you've learned these well, kept them well in mind, and you speak them clearly, with a fine voice. Memory and delivery, both. Second, where the line is. The Vinaya tells of monks who chanted the teaching in a long, drawn-out singing voice, the way songs are sung for entertainment. People complained. The Buddha forbids it and gives his reasons: the singer gets caught by the sound, the listeners do too, concentration breaks, and those who come later copy the style. Yet he allows intoning, a steady chant that carries the words. The voice serves the verse, not the other way around. Third, how long the voice carried them. The chronicle of Sri Lanka, the Mahavamsa, says that monks in earlier times passed down the texts and their commentary by mouth. Then, seeing that people were declining, they came together and wrote them down in books, so the teaching would last. Tradition holds that the elders' songs traveled that same road. Fourth, what that road asks of a voice: memory, clear speech, attention on the words. In this telling, the page came late. The verses were sung before they were written, and wherever they're chanted now, a voice still carries them.

segments.voice: Choose something short you already know, or Subhuti's lines: my hut is roofed and snug, so rain if you like. Sit up a little and say them quietly in an even voice, not performing, just carrying them, then once more, a little slower. Notice where your memory slips and where it holds, and let the words come and go with the breath.
Sarabhanna. The steady chant allowed for reciting the teaching: how the elders' songs lived first in the voice, memorized and passed mouth to ear, long before anyone wrote them down. Today's word.
Your line: sung before written. Memory and a steady voice kept these songs alive. See you tomorrow.

814.title: Your own verse
814.hook: the tradition of an awakening verse: a line spoken from what you've seen
814.howItsDone: The Udana is part of the Khuddaka Nikaya in the Pali canon; Theravada teachers draw on its stories and verses, and its opening verse is linked with the night of the awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a monk recited a chapter of verses at dawn, from memory, in sarabhanna, the steady chant. Your line was sung before written. Today, where such a verse comes from in the first place.

Then, knowing the meaning of this, on that occasion, he spoke this inspired verse. That sentence, give or take, closes story after story in a small book of the Pali canon. Something happens: monks debate which of two kings is richer, boys beat a snake with a stick, a monk sits through pain without complaint. The Buddha sees it. And a verse comes out of him, not prepared, not polished, spoken because of what he just saw. The book is named after that kind of verse.
screen: `KNOWING THE MEANING OF THIS.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS, A VERSE COMES.` → `THE BOOK IS NAMED FOR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Udana is an inspired utterance: a verse that rises out of a moment of seeing. The Udana, the book, collects them, each with its story first and its verse after. Bhaddiya, sighing ah, what bliss under his tree, is one of its stories. Second, the first one. The book opens just after the awakening. The Buddha sits under the tree, and in the first part of the night he attends to how things arise from causes. Then he speaks: when things become clear to someone ardent and absorbed, his doubts all vanish, because he understands each thing along with its cause. It isn't a hymn. It's a report of what he's just seen. Third, the elders. Their songs are not all called udanas, but tradition says the elders spoke theirs the same way, on the day something came clear: Subhuti's hut, Rahula's double fortune, Nanda's plain confession. A verse spoken from seeing, not from wishing. That's what links the book and the songs. Fourth, what it isn't. An udana isn't a prayer, and it isn't a vow. It doesn't ask for anything or promise anything. It says: this is so. And the verses in this book are brief. That leaves room for anyone who sits, at any stage, to find a line rising out of something they've actually seen. Not a verse about awakening. A verse about the rain on the roof, or the moment the anger went quiet.
screen: `A VERSE THAT RISES FROM SEEING.` · `DOUBTS VANISH, CAUSES SEEN.` · `THE ELDERS SPOKE THE SAME WAY.` · `NOT A PRAYER, NOT A VOW.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Look back over these days of sitting for a moment when something shifted, even a little: a breath that went long on its own, a thought that let go, a sound that was just a sound. Let one moment come, and let one plain sentence come out of it, from what you noticed rather than what you hope for: this is so.
Udana. An inspired utterance: a short verse spoken out of a moment of seeing, not prepared and not polished. Today's word.
Your line: this is so. A verse can be as plain as what you saw. Day eight hundred fourteen, done.

815.title: The songs, closed
815.hook: the sisters and brothers, their forests and their freedom
815.howItsDone: The Theragatha and Therigatha sit side by side in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Pali canon, and tradition hears in them the voices of the Buddha's early disciples.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was udana, a verse spoken out of a moment of seeing. Your line was this is so. Today, the songs close.

A robe sewn by hand, and someone told to sleep softly in it. A lamp's wick drawn down. A mortar, a pestle, a crooked husband, all left behind. A flower-sweeper bowed to at sunrise. A white crane flying ahead of the storm. A lute, tuned neither too tight nor too slack. Five weeks of the elders singing. Today, the last song of the block is the whole songbook, heard once more.
screen: `A WICK, A MORTAR, A LUTE.` → `FIVE WEEKS OF SONGS.` → `THE WHOLE SONGBOOK, ONCE MORE.`

segments.voice: First, the sisters. It began with the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. A nun told to sleep softly. Punna, filling herself with good things like the moon. Mutta, so freed. Patacara watching the flame go out, then teaching women who had lost their children: you don't know where he came from or where he went. Kisa Gotami's good friends. Ambapali's black hair. Subha, Punnika, Isidasi, Sumedha, each with her own long story, told her own way. Second, the brothers. Then the Theragatha, the verses of the elder monks. Subhuti's hut. The monsoon, the peacocks and the cranes. Sunita, once despised. Angulimala, the moon coming out from behind the cloud. Kassapa's hills, Sariputta's patience, Ananda's dark directions. Third, the forests. Again and again these songs are set outdoors: in groves, on rocky hills, in the rain, at the root of a tree. The freedom they describe isn't only inside a mind. It's in a place, with weather. Fourth, the freedom itself. It sounds different in each mouth. For Mutta it's leaving a kitchen. For Bhaddiya it's living without fear. For Nanda it's being pulled out of his own vanity. The collections don't flatten them into one story. They keep the names, the moods, even the complaints. What the block leaves behind is not a doctrine stated once, but a crowd of people, women and men, saying what happened to them, in verse, for whoever would listen. The elders sang.

segments.voice: From all these songs, let one singer come forward without choosing, and picture where they sit: a grove, a hut, a cell with a lamp, a hillside. Let their one line sound in you as closely as you remember it, and keep them company the way you'd sit beside an old friend who doesn't need you to talk. If you pray, hold them in your prayer; if not, just let them be near.
The songs. The verses of the elder nuns and the elder monks: forests, grief, freedom, each in its singer's own voice. Today's word.
Your line: the elders sang. They sang outdoors, under trees and open sky. See you tomorrow.

816.title: How a Jataka works
816.hook: each tale has a present story, a past story, and a last line saying who each character was
816.howItsDone: Jataka tales are retold, painted and performed in Theravada communities, and in the collection each tale closes by saying who each character was.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the songs closed, and the elders sang one last time. Your line was the elders sang. Today, a new block begins: the longer Jataka tales.

The talkative tortoise was Kokalika. The wise minister was the Bodhisatta. That's how one tale ends, in the Jataka, the great collection of stories about the Buddha's past lives. Two sentences, and suddenly a fable about a tortoise is also about a monk the listeners knew. Before the longer tales of the coming weeks, today is about the frame they share. Learn the frame once, and the tales that follow get easier to read.
screen: `THE TORTOISE WAS KOKALIKA.` → `A FABLE ABOUT SOMEONE THEY KNEW.` → `LEARN THE FRAME ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, a story in the present. A tale opens in the Buddha's own lifetime, with something that has just happened among the monks. In the tortoise tale, a monk named Kokalika has come to ruin through his own careless tongue, and the monks are talking about it. The Buddha says: this isn't the first time his tongue has brought him down. Second, a story in the past. Long ago, when a king reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha in an earlier life, was that king's minister. The king talked without stopping. Meanwhile, a tortoise made friends with two young geese, and they offered to fly him home with them, if he'd bite the middle of a stick and keep his mouth shut. Up they went. Villagers below shouted and laughed at the sight. The tortoise opened his mouth to answer back, let go of the stick, and fell into the king's courtyard. The minister used the broken tortoise to teach the king to talk less. Third, the verses. Somewhere in the tale, someone speaks a short verse, here the Bodhisatta to his king, the lesson pressed into a few lines. Fourth, who was who. Then the Buddha connects the two stories. The tortoise was Kokalika. The minister was the Bodhisatta. That last line is the hinge. It turns an old fable into a mirror: the same habits, the same people, coming round again. When you read a Jataka, you can start at the end. The last line tells you who to watch.

Then bring up one small moment from your week, a conversation, a mistake, a kindness, tell it as a tiny fable in your mind, and give it a last line: who was the tortoise there, and who was the wise minister? You might be both, so just see who was who, without judging.
Samodhana. The connection: the closing part of a Jataka where the Buddha says who was who, after a story in the present and a story in the past. Today's word.
Your line: who was who. The ending is the key to the whole tale. That's day eight hundred sixteen.

817.title: Sumedha in the mud
817.hook: a hermit lies down in the mud so the past Buddha Dipankara can walk over him, and vows to awaken (Jataka, the introduction)
817.howItsDone: In Theravada communities the story of Sumedha and Dipankara is told as the start of the Buddha's long path, and in Mahayana communities bodhisattva vows are taken in ceremonies and recited in practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: how a Jataka works, a story now, a story long ago, and the samodhana, the last line naming who was who. Your line: who was who. Today, the story the tales grow out of.

Mud. A stretch of road still soft and wet, and a Buddha walking toward it. The introduction to the Jataka opens long before Siddhartha, with a hermit named Sumedha. A city is preparing its road for the Buddha Dipankara, and Sumedha has asked for a piece of it to make smooth himself. He hasn't finished. The mud is still there when Dipankara and his monks arrive. So Sumedha does something nobody asked of him.
screen: `A ROAD NOT FINISHED.` → `A HERMIT NAMED SUMEDHA.` → `THE BUDDHA ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: First, who Sumedha was. In the story he's born rich. One day he looks at the treasure his family left him and thinks: they gathered all this, and not one of them took a coin along when they died. So he gives it away and goes to the mountains to live as a hermit. The mud scene starts with empty hands. Second, the mud. As Dipankara comes near, Sumedha loosens his hair, spreads his rough hermit's garment over the wet ground, and lies down in it, face down, so the Buddha and the monks can walk across him and keep their feet clean. Not a speech. A body on a road. Third, the choice. Lying there, the text says, Sumedha knows he could end his own suffering in this very life if he wished. He turns it down. What use is crossing over alone, he thinks. He'd rather become a Buddha himself, and carry others across with him. That's the vow: a longer road, chosen on purpose, for other people. Fourth, the answer. Dipankara stops beside him, looks far ahead, and declares that this hermit will one day be a Buddha named Gotama. The crowd hears it. Sumedha stands up. The Jataka's introduction sets the tales that follow on the long road from this vow. Mahayana traditions teach a bodhisattva vow too, in their own words and forms. Here, the road begins with a man in the dirt, and a promise said silently.

segments.voice: Choose one small vow you could actually keep, aimed at someone besides yourself: a little more room for one person, or patience with one message. Say it once, silently, the way Sumedha did in the mud, with nobody watching. Then let it go and breathe; a vow can be quiet and still be real.
Bodhisatta. The being on the way to awakening: what Sumedha vowed to become when he lay down in the mud before the Buddha Dipankara, awakening not alone, but for others. Today's word.
Your line: the vow in the mud. The longer road, chosen for others, starts with one quiet promise. Day eight hundred seventeen, done.

818.title: The ten perfections
818.hook: generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, effort, patience, truth, resolve, kindness, equanimity: Sumedha finds each one and its picture
818.howItsDone: In Theravada teaching and chanting the ten perfections are named, and the Jataka tales are taught as examples of them; Mahayana traditions teach a related list of paramitas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sumedha lay in the mud and chose the bodhisatta's longer road. Your line: the vow in the mud. Today, what he packs for that road.

A vow is a start, not a plan. In the Jataka's introduction, once the crowd has gone, Sumedha sits alone and asks a practical question: what does a person need to become a Buddha? Nobody hands him a list. He searches, the story says, and finds the qualities one at a time, each with a picture from ordinary life to hold it. The tradition calls them perfections.
screen: `A VOW, THEN A QUESTION.` → `HE SEARCHES ALONE.` → `ONE PICTURE FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Parami: the tradition uses it for a quality practiced until it's complete. Sumedha finds ten: generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, effort, patience, truth, resolve, kindness and equanimity. Second, the giving ones. Generosity is a water jar turned upside down: it pours out everything and keeps nothing back. Virtue is like a yak that guards its own tail, the story says, and would rather lose its life than lose that. Renunciation is a prisoner who has lived too long in a cell and wants only the open door. Third, the steady ones. Wisdom is a monk on alms rounds who skips no house, high or low, and learns from everyone. Effort is a lion, strong in every posture. Patience is the earth, which takes whatever is thrown on it, clean or foul, without complaint. Truth is the morning star, keeping its course in every season. Resolve is a rock mountain the wind can't move. Fourth, the warm and the even. Kindness is water, which cools the good and the bad alike. Equanimity is the earth again, unmoved by what it's handed, pleasant or not. The pictures are plain: jars, yaks, stars, water, dirt. The Jataka tales that follow are read as these ten being practiced, one life at a time. Mahayana texts teach a related list of perfections, called paramitas, with some names in common. Either way, the qualities are offered as things you build, not things you're born with.

819.title: Two caravans
819.hook: one leader trusts spirits who say to throw away the water; the other keeps it (Jataka 1)
819.howItsDone: The Apannaka Jataka stands first in the Pali Jataka collection, and Buddhist teachers tell it as a lesson in thinking a situation through before acting on persuasive advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ten perfections, a jar poured out, a star on its course, water that cools everyone. Your line: ten perfections. Today, the tale that opens the numbered collection.

Why haul all those heavy jars? There's plenty of water ahead, pools and lakes. The travelers who say it come down the desert road looking like people just out of a rainstorm: wet clothes, lotus flowers in their hair, mud on their cart wheels. They're friendly. Throw the water out, they say, and move faster. In the first tale of the Jataka, two caravans meet travelers like these. One leader listens. One doesn't.
screen: `WET CLOTHES, MUD ON THE WHEELS.` → `THROW THE WATER OUT.` → `ONE LISTENS, ONE DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: First, the two leaders. Both are merchants about to cross the same desert. One is the bodhisatta, the future Buddha. The other is a young man the tale calls foolish, eager to go first for the best grass and water. The bodhisatta lets him. Second, the first caravan. Deep in the desert, the friendly travelers appear: a demon and his followers in disguise. The young leader believes them. His people pour their water onto the sand, walk on, find no pools at all, and by night they're too weak to resist. The demons devour the caravan. Third, the second caravan. The bodhisatta meets the same strangers and the same advice. He doesn't argue or panic. He reasons. There's no rain wind blowing, no storm cloud on the horizon, and this desert is known to be dry. And these people's eyes are red and they cast no shadow, the tale says. So he tells his caravan: not one drop is to be thrown away until we see new water with our own eyes. They walk on, pass the bones of the first caravan, and cross safely. Fourth, the point. The tale doesn't praise suspicion for its own sake. It praises checking what's in front of you before trading away what keeps you alive. Advice wearing all the right costumes can still be wrong.
screen: `TWO MERCHANTS, ONE DESERT.` · `THE FIRST POURS IT OUT.` · `THE SECOND CHECKS THE SKY.` · `THE COSTUME CAN BE WRONG.` · then, large: `KEEP THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Name one plain thing that keeps you steady: sleep, a walk, ten minutes without your phone. Notice the voices that say drop it, you're too busy, there'll be plenty later, and look at the sky the way the bodhisatta did: is there really rain ahead? Then let a quiet decision settle, to keep the jar full.
Two caravans. One pours out its water on a stranger's word; one checks the sky and keeps it. Today's word.

Your line: keep the water. The week in lines: verses sung from memory, a line of your own, the songs closed, then the Jataka: who was who, a vow in the mud, ten perfections, two caravans. That's day eight hundred nineteen.
